titre: The 1935 Wagner Act Guaranteed the Right to Unionize, but Not to Everyone
accroche: On July 5, 1935, the United States recognized employees' right to unionize. The definition of employee left out farm and domestic workers.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 5, 1935, President Franklin Roosevelt signs the National Labor Relations Act, known as the Wagner Act after its sponsor, New York Senator Robert F. Wagner. The law recognized employees' right to organize in unions and gave a federal agency the means to enforce it.

## A Right, a Procedure, a Judge

Section 7 set out the rights: to form labor organizations, to join or assist them, to bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and to act together for mutual aid. Section 8 listed the *unfair labor practices* forbidden to employers: interfering with these rights, dominating or financing a union, punishing an employee for union membership or for filing a complaint, refusing to bargain with the chosen representatives. Section 3 provided for a National Labor Relations Board of three members, appointed by the president with the consent of the Senate. It determined bargaining units, held representation elections, investigated complaints, and could order violations to stop.

The law still has to pass the test of the Constitution. On April 12, 1937, in *NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp.*, the United States Supreme Court declares it constitutional.

## Who Is an "Employee"?

Each of these rights is granted to a holder: the *employee*. It is section 2(3) that defines the term, and it carves out entire categories. The English text excludes "any individual employed as an agricultural laborer, or in the domestic service of any family or person at his home," that is, the farm worker and the person employed in a household's domestic service. These workers did not fall under the Board: no complaint to file there, no election to request.

The text gives no reasons for these exclusions. Juan Perea, in a 2011 article in the *Ohio State Law Journal* titled *The Echoes of Slavery*, reads a racial origin into them: the title states the thesis. This entry reports that reading without settling it, and otherwise sticks to what the text establishes.

## The Shift

The Wagner Act is sometimes summed up as the law that gave Americans the right to unionize. The text says more narrowly: it gave it to the people it called *employees*. Between the right in general and the right of this law lies a definition of a few lines. A right is never only what it proclaims. It is also the set of people its definition of the holder leaves outside.

When a right is presented as universal, what holder does its definition assume?

repere.texte: Section 2(3) of the July 5, 1935 law excludes from the definition of employee persons employed as agricultural laborers or "in the domestic service of any family or person at his home."
repere.source: National Labor Relations Act (1935), Milestone Documents, National Archives

carte.punch: The 1935 law on union rights left out farm and domestic workers.
carte.idee: The Wagner Act (July 5, 1935) recognized American employees' right to organize. But this right belonged to "employees," whom section 2(3) defined by excluding agricultural and domestic workers: the list of those left out mattered as much as the proclamation.

quiz.question: Why could a farm worker not bring a case before the National Labor Relations Board under the 1935 law?
choix: Because the Supreme Court had ruled in 1935 that agriculture fell outside commerce between the states
Because these rights were reserved for "employees," and section 2(3) excluded him from the definition
Because the law applied only to factories of more than a hundred employees located in large cities
Because agriculture already had its own board created by another law passed the same year
quiz.explication: The protections of sections 7 and 8 benefited "employees," and section 2(3) removed farm and domestic workers from that definition. The exclusion is in the law's own definition; the other answers put forward reasons the text does not give.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the National Labor Relations Board provided for by section 3 of the 1935 law do?
choix: It itself set the minimum wage for each occupation across the whole country
It found companies guilty of illegal strikes and sentenced them to heavy fines
It held representation elections and investigated complaints of unfair practices in businesses
It appointed the leaders of recognized unions after a vote by the employees concerned
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Board determines bargaining units, holds representation elections, investigates complaints, and can order violations to stop. The other tasks cited do not appear in section 3.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Supreme Court establish on April 12, 1937 in NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin Steel Corp.?
choix: It confirms that the 1935 law is constitutional
It strikes down the 1935 law as exceeding Congress's powers
It extends the law to farm and domestic workers
It transfers control of the law to the states
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1937 Court upholds the law. The other answers describe decisions this ruling did not make.
